title: Query optimisation: plan space
lead: Parsing, rewriting, algebraic equivalences, pushdown and physical alternatives.

sections.title: Query optimisation and query lifecycle
sections.html:
Optimisation goal and strategy families

This four-up PDF page shows the title and printed slides 2–4. Optimisation bridges a declarative query and an imperative implementation. The objective is the lowest estimated cost among correct candidate plans; huge search spaces and uncertain estimates prevent a general promise of the true optimum.

The source focuses on Selinger/System R and mentions Volcano/Cascades, stratified search, randomised search and AI-driven approaches. These are strategy families, not interchangeable names for one algorithm. Avoiding a catastrophic plan is often more practical than exhaustively proving optimality.

PDF p. 1

Parser, query blocks and sound simplification

Printed slides 5–8 show parser → rewriter → cost-based optimiser → executor, with catalog schema/statistics support. The parser checks syntax, attribute resolution, types and authorisation and forms SELECT-FROM-WHERE query blocks, whose FROM items can themselves be subqueries.

The rewriter can replace WHERE 1=0 by an empty result and WHERE 1=1 by no filter. For R(id PRIMARY KEY,val NOT NULL), the self-join R1.id=R2.id selecting only R1 columns can be eliminated because every R1 row has exactly one counterpart. Without uniqueness or the required output projection, that rewrite may change multiplicity.

PDF p. 2

sections.title: Plan space and algebraic equivalences
sections.html:
Subquery removal, predicate merging and search components

The displayed printed numbers are 9,10,12,14; 11 and 13 are absent from this supplied PDF. A self-correlated EXISTS on the same table’s primary key is always satisfied for an outer row and can be removed. The union of val BETWEEN 1 AND 100 with val BETWEEN 50 AND 150 is the continuous interval 1…150 under the stated semantics.

The optimiser enumerates promising physical plans, estimates their costs from catalog data and selects per block. Plan space defines allowed alternatives, cost estimation ranks them and search strategy decides which to inspect. A larger space can contain better plans but costs more to search.

PDF p. 3

Equivalence laws and join-reordering pitfalls

Printed slides 15–18 give selection cascade/commutativity, safe projection cascade and product associativity/commutativity. Keep every column needed by a later predicate. Algebraic inner-join reordering must move predicates with the attributes they reference.

For R(A,Y),S(A,B),T(B,Z), a join between T and R cannot apply S.A=R.A because S is absent. Replacing that inner join with T×R but dropping the A predicate is also wrong. The correct outer join against S must test both S.B=T.B and S.A=R.A. Attribute availability and predicate preservation establish equivalence; tree shape alone does not.

PDF p. 4

sections.title: Selection and projection pushdown
sections.html:
Transitivity and selection pushdown

Printed slides 19–22 derive R.A=T.C from R.A=S.B and S.B=T.C, enabling R⋈T without a product. Split conjunctive predicates and push each to the earliest node containing its attributes. X=Y AND Y=3 can expose X=3; arithmetic rewrites require compatible types, overflow and NULL semantics.

In the source Reserves/Sailors plan, bid=100 belongs on Reserves and rating>5 on Sailors before their sid join. This reduces join input cardinalities. It does not necessarily reduce base pages read or repeated inner-scan I/O; the next lecture calculates those effects.

PDF p. 5

Projection, products and heuristic limits

Printed slides 23–26 retain sid on Reserves and sid,sname on Sailors after filtering, because sid joins and sname is output. Narrowing tuples can reduce intermediate pages; SQL bag projections must preserve multiplicity rather than silently performing set DISTINCT.

Avoid products when a connected join is available, but the source gives an exception: if R and T are tiny relative to S, a small R×T intermediate can be competitive. Heuristics prune candidates, not prove the cheapest result. Physical implementations must be considered after logical rewrites.

PDF p. 6

sections.title: Physical plan alternatives
sections.html:
Physical alternatives and the role of costing

Printed slides 27–28 enumerate heap/index access and block nested-loop, indexed nested-loop, sort-merge and Grace hash implementations for suitable joins. General non-equality joins need an implementation supporting their predicate, such as block nested loops.

The plan space combines logical rewrites with those choices. Their costs depend on cardinality, tuple widths, indexes, ordering, buffers and materialisation. Early filtering is often useful, but selecting the best full plan requires consistent cost accounting. Physical PDF pages 1–7 here correspond to multiple displayed printed slides, so the two numbering schemes are deliberately recorded separately.

PDF p. 7

quiz.question: Which columns must projection pushdown retain?
options: Only the columns in the final SELECT list
Output columns and every column still needed by later operators
quiz.explanation: Join keys and filter columns remain necessary even when they are absent from the final SELECT list.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes the parser, rewriter, and cost-based optimizer; query blocks and the System R approach; logical equivalences and safe simplifications; join reordering, cross products, and transitive predicates; selection and projection pushdown; and physical implementation choices. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
